newsitem.title: GERMANY: Blair to Kohl - reform your economy for EMU's sake.
newsitem.headline: Blair to Kohl - reform your economy for EMU's sake.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair, Europe's youngest prime minister, flew into Bonn on Friday with firm but polite advice for Europe's elder statesman, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl: modernise your economy if you want the single currency to work.

Fresh from warning Europe's centre-left parties at a congress in Sweden of the need to ditch outdated economic ideas, Blair was due to deliver a similar message to Kohl in their first face-to-face talks.
To make sure his point got across to German voters, Blair said the same in a front-page commentary in the country's most popular newspaper, the mass circulation Bild daily.

Speaking to reporters during his flight from a European socialist party meeting in Malmo in southern Sweden, Blair said: "In order to make the single market work and certainly if Europe proceeds towards a single currncy, you have got to have the economies in proper shape.

"That means flexible labour makets, investment in education and skills and ensuring that we're developing the type of welfare state that is compatible with what is a completely different set of economic conditions today."

Aides said Blair won strong support for his ideas during bilateral meetings in Malmo with the prime ministers of Sweden and Denmark but was under no illusion that it would take time to convince Germany of the need to reform.

Commentators in Germany sometimes say Blair is to the right of Kohl, whose Christian Democratic Union (CDU) supports a "social market economy" with elements of intervention that look more like traditional social democratic policy that New Labour.

"I think we are building support for a genuine new third way in Europe, which means the role of government is not old-style state intervention or heaping regulations on employers -- but neither is it the way of conservative parties of simply letting people sink or swim in the market place," Blair said.
"The new way is about education, skills, new technology, developing small busnesses and equipping people to survive in a completely different set of economic conditions.
"I believe there is a lot of support for that right across Europe," Blair said.

Asked whether the single currency risked becoming a potentially disastrous irrelevance, Blair -- who says it is highly unlikely Britain will join monetary union (EMU) at the start -- said it was up to Germany to decide whether it wanted to press ahead with the project.
"If the single currency is fudged or the criteria for it are fiddled, or we don't take the measures of reform that we are suggesting in Europe... then there will be problems," he said.

Blair said it was up to each country to decide whether to sign up for EMU. "But all countries have got a common interest in making sure we reform the economies of Europe to make us more competitive for the future," he said.
